title: Tests for ions; Aldehydes and ketones
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for OCR A-level (A) Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: PT07#t1 term and clue written for the game; OR17a#t3 term and clue written for the game; PT07#t3 term and clue written for the game; OR17a#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: OR17a#N.6, PT07#N.3, OR17a#N.9, PT07#N.6, OR17a#N.12, PT07#N.14a.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Cation
items.clue: The positive particle in a salt, such as Ba²⁺.

items.label: Ketone
items.clue: Has C=O inside the chain rather than at its end, as in propanone.

items.label: Limewater
items.clue: Turns milky when CO₂ from a carbonate and dilute acid is bubbled in.

items.label: Aldehyde
items.clue: Has C=O at the end of the chain with an H on it; the name ends in -al.

questions.stem: Butanone, CH₃COCH₂CH₃, is reduced. Reagent: NaBH₄(aq). What is the organic product?

options.text: Butan-1-ol
Butane
Butan-2-ol
Butanoic acid

questions.explanation: CH₃COCH₂CH₃ + 2[H] → CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃. A ketone gives a secondary alcohol.

questions.stem: Which result shows that a solid contains ammonium ions?

options.text: Dilute hydrochloric acid is added; a gas forms that turns limewater milky.
It is warmed with NaOH(aq); a gas forms that turns damp red litmus paper blue.
NaOH(aq) is added to its solution; a white precipitate forms that stays on warming.
Its solution turns damp blue litmus paper red, and no gas forms on warming.

questions.explanation: OH⁻ ions remove H⁺ from NH₄⁺, releasing ammonia, the only common alkaline gas.

questions.stem: In the mechanism for the reaction of propanone with cyanide, where does the first curly arrow start and end?

options.text: From the lone pair on the N of CN⁻ to the carbonyl carbon
From the lone pair on the C of CN⁻ to the carbonyl carbon
From the C=O π bond to the C of CN⁻
From a lone pair on the carbonyl O to H⁺

questions.explanation: The cyanide carbon's lone pair forms the new C–C bond to the δ+ carbonyl carbon.

questions.stem: A student adds barium chloride solution to a solution of an unknown sodium salt, without adding acid first. A white precipitate forms. Why can the student not yet conclude that sulfate ions are present?

options.text: Barium chloride gives a white precipitate with every negative ion.
The white solid could be sodium chloride crystallising out of the mixture.
The solid could be barium carbonate, which acid would have prevented.
Barium ions react with water to form a white barium hydroxide precipitate.

questions.explanation: BaCO₃ is also white and insoluble. Dilute HCl first removes carbonate as CO₂, so a white precipitate after acidifying must be BaSO₄.

questions.stem: Hex-5-en-2-one, CH₂=CHCH₂CH₂COCH₃, has a C=C bond and a C=O bond. It is warmed with NaBH₄(aq). What is the organic product?

options.text: Hex-5-en-2-ol, CH₂=CHCH₂CH₂CH(OH)CH₃
Hexan-2-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH(OH)CH₃
Hexan-2-one, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂COCH₃
Hex-5-en-1-ol, CH₂=CHCH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂OH

questions.explanation: H⁻ is a nucleophile. It attacks the δ+ carbon of C=O. The non-polar, electron-rich C=C does not attract it.

questions.stem: A garden-centre sack of white fertiliser crystals has lost its label. It could be ammonium sulfate, ammonium carbonate, ammonium chloride or potassium sulfate. Which pair of results shows it is ammonium sulfate?

options.text: Warming with NaOH(aq) gives a gas that turns damp red litmus blue; BaCl₂(aq) gives a white precipitate that fizzes and dissolves when dilute HCl is added.
Warming with NaOH(aq) gives no alkaline gas; dilute HCl then BaCl₂(aq) gives a white precipitate.
Warming with NaOH(aq) gives a gas that turns damp red litmus blue; dilute HCl then BaCl₂(aq) gives a white precipitate.
Warming with NaOH(aq) gives a gas that turns damp red litmus blue; dilute HNO₃ then AgNO₃(aq) gives a white precipitate.
